sections.title: Introduction
key_points: Introduces the chapter on distribution of stresses
Contains subsections on scope and state of stress
sections.applicability: General introduction to the chapter on stress distribution in soil.

sections.title: Scope
sections.body: This chapter describes the analysis of stress conditions within the ground, including stress at a point, changes in stress caused by the application of soil and structural loads, and empirical methods for estimating loads on buried pipes, conduits, shafts, and tunnels. The calculation of stresses and changes in stress using numerical methods, such as the finite element method, is also discussed.
key_points: Covers stress at a point and changes in stress from soil and structural loads
Includes empirical methods for loads on buried pipes, conduits, shafts, and tunnels
Discusses numerical methods including the finite element method
sections.applicability: Defines the overall scope of Chapter 4, applicable to all stress distribution analyses in geotechnical engineering.

sections.title: State of Stress
sections.body:
The state of stress within the ground can be analyzed assuming that either elastic or plastic conditions prevail. Elastic solutions are most appropriate for cases in which the shear stresses throughout the soil mass are significantly below the shear strength of the soil and shear failure is not likely. If the shear stress in the soil is less than about one-third of the ultimate shear strength, the stresses within the soil mass will be roughly equal to values calculated from elastic theory (Davis and Selvadurai 1996). The stress conditions calculated using the most of the methods in this chapter assume that elastic conditions prevail.

Plastic solutions assume full mobilization of the soil's shear strength within a soil mass or along a specified failure surface. Plastic equilibrium is used for problems, such as slope stability (Chapter 7), foundation bearing capacity, and lateral earth pressures, where shear strength may be fully mobilized.
key_points: Elastic solutions apply when shear stress is significantly below the shear strength
If shear stress is less than about one-third of ultimate shear strength, elastic theory gives reasonable results
Most methods in this chapter assume elastic conditions
Plastic solutions assume full mobilization of shear strength and are used for slope stability, bearing capacity, and lateral earth pressures
sections.applicability: Applies when determining whether elastic or plastic stress analysis methods are appropriate for a given soil stress condition.

sections.title: Stress Conditions at a Point
key_points: Parent section for subsections on stress conditions in soil and Mohr circle of stress
sections.applicability: General section heading for stress conditions at a point within the ground.

sections.title: Stress Conditions in Soil
sections.body:
Soil consists of a compilation of discrete particles, water, and air in varying proportions. Similarly, rock may contain a combination of the mineral components and any void space that may be filled with water or air. These discrete systems are idealized in stress analysis by assuming the soil acts as continuous solid mass without holes or gaps. In this continuum manner, stress is simply conceived as force per unit area and the contact forces at the soil particle level are not considered.

Stress in soil is the result of forces from the self-weight of the overlying and surrounding soil plus any external loading, such as structures or ponded water. For a given plane, it can be particularly useful to consider stress in terms of its normal and shear components. The normal stress can be defined as the sum of the forces acting perpendicular to a plane divided by the area of that plane. Similarly shear stress in a particular direction is ratio of the force acting tangent to a plane divided by its area.

The total normal stress on any plane within the ground is based on the sum of all forces acting on the plane in question. The total stress may be divided into two parts: the effective normal stress and the pore pressure.
key_points: Soil is idealized as a continuous solid mass for stress analysis
Stress is conceived as force per unit area in the continuum approach
Stress results from self-weight of soil and external loading
Normal stress is force perpendicular to a plane divided by area; shear stress is tangential force divided by area
Total normal stress is divided into effective normal stress and pore pressure
sections.applicability: Applies to the conceptual framework for analyzing stress in soil as a continuum.

sections.title: Total Vertical Stress
sections.body:
The total vertical stress (or overburden stress) is the normal stress acting on a horizontal plane at some depth within the soil. The total vertical stress, sigma_v, at a particular depth is calculated by multiplying the thickness (zi) of all overlying materials by the total unit weight (gamma_t,i) of each material:

sigma_v = sum from i=1 to n of (zi * gamma_t,i)  (4-1)

It is imperative to include the weight of water resting on the ground surface (i.e., ponded water) in calculations of total vertical stress. Ponded water can be considered by adding a layer to the total stress calculations with thickness equal to the water depth and unit weight equal to the unit weight of water.

The calculation of total vertical stress is illustrated in Figure 4-1.
key_points: Total vertical stress is the normal stress on a horizontal plane at depth
Calculated by summing the product of layer thickness and total unit weight for all overlying materials
Ponded water must be included in total vertical stress calculations
Ponded water is treated as a layer with thickness equal to water depth and unit weight of water

equations.description: Calculates total vertical stress as the summation of layer thickness times total unit weight for all overlying materials

figures: Figure 4-1: Calculation of Vertical Stresses for Hydrostatic Conditions
sections.applicability: Applies to calculation of total vertical (overburden) stress at any depth in a soil profile, including cases with ponded water.

sections.title: Pore Water Pressure
sections.body:
The energy present in ponded water or groundwater is often expressed in terms of the total hydraulic head, which has pressure, elevation, and velocity components. The velocity component is typically ignored in most geotechnical applications. The pore water pressure (u) can be found from the pressure head (hp) as

u = hp * gamma_w  (4-2)

where gamma_w = the unit weight of water (62.4 pcf or 9.81 kN/m3).

When water is static (not flowing), the total head is constant throughout the system, and elevation head converts directly to pressure head. This is referred to as a hydrostatic condition, and the pressure head is simply equal to the distance below the groundwater table or phreatic surface.

Flowing water loses energy as it flows through the soil and the total head decreases in the direction of flow. For flowing water conditions, a flow net or some other type of seepage analysis must be performed. Pore water pressure at any point can be determined by first calculating the total head and the elevation head at any point in the ground. The pressure head for flowing water is found by subtracting the elevation head from the total head. Water pressures act in all directions equally because the water does not sustain shear stress. For this reason, orientation of the pore water pressure is not important. In some older publications, pore water pressure is also called neutral stress.
key_points: Pore water pressure is calculated from pressure head times the unit weight of water
Velocity component of hydraulic head is typically ignored in geotechnical applications
Under hydrostatic conditions, pressure head equals the distance below the water table
For flowing water, a seepage analysis is required to determine pore water pressure
Water pressure acts equally in all directions because water does not sustain shear stress
Pore water pressure is also historically called neutral stress

equations.description: Calculates pore water pressure from the pressure head multiplied by the unit weight of water

sections.applicability: Applies to the determination of pore water pressure under both hydrostatic and flowing water conditions in soil.

sections.title: Effective Vertical Stress
sections.body:
The effective vertical stress (sigma'_v) is found by subtracting the pore water pressure at any point from the total vertical stress at the same point

sigma'_v = sigma_v - u  (4-3).
key_points: Effective vertical stress equals total vertical stress minus pore water pressure
This is the fundamental effective stress relationship for vertical stress

equations.description: Calculates effective vertical stress by subtracting pore water pressure from total vertical stress

sections.applicability: Applies to the calculation of effective vertical stress at any point in a saturated or partially saturated soil profile.

sections.title: Horizontal Stress
sections.body:
Horizontal stress in a soil mass is influenced by the effective vertical stress, the geologic stress history, and lateral confinement conditions. Horizontal stress cannot be calculated directly from the soil profile and is typically calculated as a proportion of the effective vertical stress:

sigma'_h = K * sigma'_v  (4-4).

The lateral earth pressure coefficient (K) depends on stress history and lateral confinement conditions. Common types, applications, and sources of lateral earth pressure coefficients are summarized in Table 4-1.

The total horizontal stress can be found by adding the pore water pressure at any point onto the effective horizontal stress

sigma_h = sigma'_h + u  (4-5).
key_points: Horizontal stress depends on effective vertical stress, geologic stress history, and lateral confinement
Effective horizontal stress is calculated as a proportion of effective vertical stress using the lateral earth pressure coefficient K
K depends on stress history and confinement conditions (at-rest, active, or passive)
Total horizontal stress is the effective horizontal stress plus pore water pressure

equations.description: Calculates effective horizontal stress as the lateral earth pressure coefficient times the effective vertical stress
Calculates total horizontal stress by adding pore water pressure to effective horizontal stress

sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of horizontal stresses in soil based on effective vertical stress and lateral earth pressure coefficients.

sections.title: Applied Loads
sections.body:
Many civil engineering applications must consider the effects of external (non-soil) loads applied at the surface or at some depth within the soil mass. The influence of existing loads must be included in total stress calculations. New loads cause changes in total stress within the soil. These load changes will cause changes in the pore water pressures as discussed in more detail in Chapter 5. The duration of the changes in pore water pressure will depend on the permeability and compressibility of the soil.

Analytical methods for calculating changes in stress are provided in Section 4-3, including methods for point loads, line loads, and uniformly loaded areas. In Section 4-6, numerical methods for calculating changes in stress are summarized.

Changes in total stress caused by applied loads should be within the soil mass to at least the critical depth. The critical depth is the depth over which soil compression caused by the changes in stress contributes to significant surface settlement. The critical depth in fine-grained soils corresponds to the depth at which the change in stress is less than 10% of the existing vertical effective stress. In coarse-grained soils, the critical depth occurs when the change in stress is less than 20% of the existing vertical effective stress.

Interactions between the applied load and the soil foundation must be considered, especially for changes in stress very close to the load. The flexibility of the structure that applies a distributed load to the soil affects the distribution of the change in stress. A completely flexible load, such as a soil fill, will apply a uniform stress to the soil because the load can deform in proportion to the soil. The elastic solutions presented in Section 4-3 assume that the load is completely flexible.

A foundation that is completely rigid with respect to the soil must undergo a uniform deformation. When a rigid foundation deforms uniformly into an elastic solid (i.e., undrained conditions for clay), the load must shift to the edges of the foundation, resulting in a pressure distribution that increases toward the edge (see Figure 4-2). In contrast, a rigid foundation on sand will cause yielding near the edges, resulting a pressure distribution that decreases toward the edge.
key_points: External loads cause changes in total stress and pore water pressure within the soil
Critical depth in fine-grained soils is where change in stress is less than 10% of existing effective vertical stress
Critical depth in coarse-grained soils is where change in stress is less than 20% of existing effective vertical stress
Completely flexible loads apply uniform stress; elastic solutions in Section 4-3 assume flexible loading
Rigid foundations on elastic soil (clay) cause stress concentration at the edges
Rigid foundations on sand cause yielding near edges with stress decreasing toward the edge
figures: Figure 4-2: Variation in Contact Pressure – a) Rigid Foundation and b) Completely Flexible Foundation
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating changes in stress from external loads on soil, including considerations of foundation rigidity and critical depth.

sections.title: Mohr Circle of Stress
sections.body:
The normal and shear stress on a plane at any point within the ground depends on the orientation of that plane with respect to the orientation of the stress system. At any point, the will be three mutually perpendicular planes that have no shear stress, which are referred to as the principal planes. The normal stresses that act on these planes are defined as the principal stresses. The major principal stress (sigma_1) has the largest magnitude. The minor principal stress (sigma_3) has the smallest magnitude. The intermediate principal stress (sigma_2) falls between sigma_1 and sigma_3. For two-dimensional problems, sigma_2 is either assumed equal to sigma_3 or ignored. For level ground conditions, the principal stresses are often assumed to be aligned with the horizontal and vertical directions with the horizontal normal stress being equal in all directions. The sign convention used herein assigns positive values to compressive stress, shear stress that causes counterclockwise rotation, and counterclockwise angles.

A Mohr circle of stress can easily be plotted from sigma_1 and sigma_3, or the normal and shear stresses on any two perpendicular planes. More information on the use of the Mohr circle can be found in Parry (2004). From the Mohr circle for a point, the normal and shear stress conditions on any plane can be determined by rotating an angle 2*alpha about the center of the circle, where alpha is the angle between the major principal plane and the plane of interest. Figure 4-3 illustrates the Mohr circle and mathematical relationships between common stresses.
key_points: Normal and shear stress on a plane depend on the orientation of the plane relative to the stress system
Principal planes have no shear stress; principal stresses act on these planes
Major (sigma_1), intermediate (sigma_2), and minor (sigma_3) principal stresses are defined
For 2D problems, sigma_2 is assumed equal to sigma_3 or ignored
Sign convention: positive for compressive stress, counterclockwise shear stress, and counterclockwise angles
Mohr circle allows determination of stress on any plane by rotating angle 2*alpha about the circle center
sections.applicability: Applies to the graphical and analytical determination of stress on any plane at a point using Mohr circle construction.

sections.title: Elastic Solutions for Stresses Due to Applied Loads
key_points: Parent section for elastic stress distribution solutions including Boussinesq and Westergaard methods
sections.applicability: General section heading for elastic methods of calculating stress changes due to applied loads.

sections.title: Use and Applicability
sections.body: The elastic solutions presented in this section are useful for simple analyses of changes in stress, especially consolidation settlement. These methods are also useful for understanding the principles of stress distribution and for checking more complicated numerical analyses.
key_points: Elastic solutions are useful for simple stress change analyses, especially consolidation settlement
Useful for understanding stress distribution principles
Useful for checking more complicated numerical analyses
sections.applicability: Applies when simple elastic solutions are needed for stress change analysis or for verification of numerical models.

sections.title: Semi-Infinite Elastic Conditions
key_points: Parent section covering Boussinesq-type solutions for homogeneous, semi-infinite elastic media
sections.applicability: General section heading for Boussinesq and related elastic solutions for semi-infinite soil media.

sections.title: Assumptions
sections.body: The Boussinesq and related solutions assume the soil is a homogeneous, elastic material in which continuity is maintained and static equilibrium is satisfied. The applied load is completely flexible and is applied at the surface of the material. For embankment loading, the load is strictly vertical and no shear stress is applied to the foundation by the embankment. As discussed in Section 4-2.1.5, the stress distribution below a rigid foundation is not uniform and may not conform to the assumptions of the Boussinesq solutions.
key_points: Boussinesq assumes homogeneous, elastic, continuous material with static equilibrium
Applied load is completely flexible and applied at the surface
Embankment loading is strictly vertical with no shear stress applied to the foundation
Stress distribution below rigid foundations is not uniform and may not conform to Boussinesq assumptions
sections.applicability: Applies when using Boussinesq solutions; soil must be approximately homogeneous, elastic, and the load must be flexible and surface-applied.

sections.title: Stress Distribution Formulas
sections.body:
Formulas for homogeneous, semi-infinite, isotropic foundations are summarized in Table 4-2. These formulas can be used for hand calculations for simple computations and to check the results of more complex numerical analyses. Such formulas can also easily be programmed into a spreadsheet solution. Additional formulas for other geometric and loading conditions are summarized in Poulos and Davis (1974).

Horizontal and shear stresses caused by applied loads can also be determined from elastic solutions. In many cases, these calculations require a value of Poisson's ratio (nu) for the soil. Many of the common figures assume nu = 0.5 making it important to verify the value of nu that was used. One application of horizontal stress calculations is for the loading of unyielding walls as discussed in DM 7.2. For conditions where elastic solutions are suitable, the calculation of shear stress is typically not required.

Loads with a length to width ratio (L/B) of at least five are commonly assumed to result in plane strain conditions, at least near the middle of the length. Under plane strain, deformation only occurs perpendicular to the long axis of the load and the changes in stress do not depend on the elastic properties of the material.

The Boussinesq solutions are not typically applicable to the calculation of shear stress for conditions where shear stress is becoming critical. In this case, the soil is approaching a state of plastic equilibrium and the assumption of elasticity no longer applies. In such cases, stability analysis methods, such as those in Chapter 7 and in DM 7.2, should be used.
key_points: Table 4-2 summarizes formulas for vertical stress under various loading conditions on semi-infinite, isotropic foundations
Formulas are suitable for hand calculations and spreadsheet programming
Horizontal and shear stress calculations may require Poisson's ratio; many charts assume nu = 0.5
Loads with L/B >= 5 are commonly assumed to produce plane strain conditions
Boussinesq solutions are not applicable when shear stress approaches critical (plastic equilibrium) conditions
Stability analysis methods should be used when shear failure is possible
tables: Table 4-2: Equations for the Calculation of Change in Vertical Stress Below Various Loading Conditions
sections.applicability: Applies to hand calculations and spreadsheet solutions for changes in vertical stress under simple loading conditions on homogeneous, isotropic, semi-infinite elastic foundations.

sections.title: Chart Solutions for Vertical Stress beneath Regular Loads
sections.body:
Figure 4-4 to Figure 4-7 provide chart solutions for regularly shaped loads and Boussinesq theory. These charts are all based on the assumption of nu = 0.5, where required, to determine the change in vertical stress. Example calculations are provided in Figure 4-9. Additional guidance on the calculation of changes in stress under elastic conditions can be found in Poulos and Davis (1974).

In the past, changes in stress caused by irregularly shaped loaded areas were calculated using chart solutions such as those proposed by Newmark (1942) and Jimenez Salas (1948). However, for complex loading conditions, numerical analysis has become the most common means to evaluate changes in stress.
key_points: Figures 4-4 through 4-7 provide Boussinesq chart solutions for strip, square, rectangular, circular, and embankment loads
Charts assume Poisson's ratio of 0.5
Example calculations are provided in Figure 4-9
Newmark and Jimenez Salas chart solutions were historically used for irregularly shaped loads
Numerical analysis is now the preferred method for complex loading conditions
figures: Figure 4-4: Vertical Stress Contours from Strip and Square Loaded Areas – Boussinesq
Figure 4-5: Influence Factors for a Rectangular Loaded Area – Boussinesq
Figure 4-6: Influence Factors for a Circular Loaded Area – Boussinesq (after Ahlvin and Ulery 1962, Poulos and Davis 1974)
Figure 4-7: Influence Factors for Embankment Loading – Boussinesq (after Poulos and Davis 1974)
sections.applicability: Applies when using chart-based Boussinesq solutions for changes in vertical stress beneath regularly shaped loaded areas assuming Poisson's ratio of 0.5.

sections.title: Superposition
sections.body: The assumption of linear elasticity inherent in the Boussinesq solutions allows for superposition of stresses that result from applied loads. This means that the change in stress from one load can be added or subtracted from those caused by other loads, provided the same point is being considered in all cases. This principle is especially useful for determining the change in stress below and outside of loaded areas as illustrated in Figure 4-8.
key_points: Linear elasticity allows superposition of stresses from multiple applied loads
Changes in stress from individual loads can be added or subtracted at the same point
Superposition is especially useful for determining stress changes below and outside loaded areas
figures: Figure 4-8: Use of Superposition to Determine Change in Vertical Stress
sections.applicability: Applies when combining stress changes from multiple loads using Boussinesq elastic solutions.

sections.title: St. Venant's Principle
sections.body: St. Venant's principle is another useful concept for the calculation of change in stress due to applied loads. According to this principle, the change in stress caused by two statically equivalent loads becomes equal as the distance from the load becomes sufficiently large. Practically, this means that a square or circular load can be replaced with a point load, or a strip load can be considered a line load. It is commonly assumed that St. Venant's principle can be applied to the calculation of change in vertical stress, delta_sigma_z, for depths greater than three times the width of the applied load.
key_points: St. Venant's principle states that statically equivalent loads produce equal stress changes at sufficient distance
A square or circular load can be replaced with a point load at sufficient depth
A strip load can be treated as a line load at sufficient depth
Commonly applied for depths greater than three times the width of the applied load
sections.applicability: Applies when simplifying loaded area geometry for stress calculations at depths greater than three times the load width.

sections.title: Layered or Anisotropic Foundations
sections.body: While the Boussinesq solutions offer a relatively simple means to calculate changes in stress, soil is not a homogeneous, isotropic, and semi-infinite medium. For example, different layers typically have different values of elastic modulus. Soil layers are often more rigid horizontally than vertically. These deviations from the assumptions of Boussinesq have led to the development of other methods for the calculation of changes in stress, most notably the Westergaard type of analysis.
key_points: Soil is not truly homogeneous, isotropic, and semi-infinite as Boussinesq assumes
Different layers have different elastic moduli and soil is often more rigid horizontally than vertically
Westergaard analysis was developed to address these deviations from Boussinesq assumptions
sections.applicability: Applies to layered or anisotropic soil profiles where Boussinesq assumptions are not met.

sections.title: Westergaard Analysis
sections.body: Westergaard analysis assumes that the soil below the load is reinforced by closely spaced horizontal layers that prevent horizontal displacement. This reinforcement effect causes the changes in stress predicted by Westergaard to be less than those calculated by the Boussinesq assumptions. The Westergaard type of analysis is most appropriate for soil profiles that have alternating layers of stiff and soft soils, such as soft clay with intermittent horizontal layers of sand. Figure 4-10 provides influence factors for points below the corner of a rectangular loaded area, assuming Westergaard theory.
key_points: Westergaard assumes soil is reinforced by closely spaced horizontal layers preventing horizontal displacement
Westergaard predicts smaller changes in stress than Boussinesq
Most appropriate for profiles with alternating stiff and soft layers (e.g., soft clay with sand layers)
Figure 4-10 provides influence factors for rectangular loaded areas using Westergaard theory
figures: Figure 4-10: Influence Factors for a Rectangular Loaded Area – Westergaard
sections.applicability: Applies to soil profiles with alternating layers of stiff and soft soils where horizontal displacement is restrained.

sections.title: Layered Foundations
sections.body: Soil profiles may have layers of significant thickness and very different elastic properties. The changes vertical stress induced in these cases differs significantly from that predicted by Boussinesq assumptions. Analytical and chart-based solutions have been suggested to account for such differences using rigidity factors (e.g., Mehta and Veletsos 1959). For these conditions, numerical analysis is the preferred method to determine changes in stress or as a means of comparison to simpler solutions.
key_points: Layered profiles with significantly different elastic properties deviate from Boussinesq predictions
Rigidity factor approaches have been proposed (e.g., Mehta and Veletsos 1959)
Numerical analysis is the preferred method for layered foundation stress calculations
sections.applicability: Applies to soil profiles with layers of significant thickness and very different elastic properties.

sections.title: Shallow Pipes and Conduits
key_points: Parent section for methods to determine stresses on shallow buried pipes and conduits
sections.applicability: General section heading for stress analysis of shallow buried pipes and conduits.

sections.title: General
sections.body:
The stresses on shallow pipes and conduits due to applied loads is one important application of concepts presented in this chapter. The factors influencing these stresses include the relative rigidity of the pipe to the soil, the depth of cover, the type of loading, the maximum width (span) of the structure, the method of construction, and the shape of the pipe.

This section presents simple empirical procedures based on observations. More detailed analysis can be conducted numerically or by consulting Moser (1990) or American Lifelines Alliance (2001).
key_points: Stresses on pipes depend on relative pipe-soil rigidity, depth of cover, loading type, span, construction method, and pipe shape
Simple empirical procedures based on observations are presented
More detailed analysis can use numerical methods or references by Moser (1990) and American Lifelines Alliance (2001)
sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of stresses on shallow buried pipes and conduits from applied loads.

sections.title: Vertical Loads on Rigid Pipe
sections.body: Rigid pipes are those made of precast concrete, cast-in-place concrete, or cast iron.
key_points: Rigid pipes include precast concrete, cast-in-place concrete, and cast iron pipes
sections.applicability: Applies to vertical load estimation on rigid pipes made of precast concrete, cast-in-place concrete, or cast iron.

sections.title: Dead Load
sections.body:
Estimates of the load caused by vertical stress on a rigid pipe can be made using the approach suggested by Marston and Anderson (1913) and subsequent work by Spangler (1948). The load per length of pipe (Wd) in a trench can be calculated as:

Wd = Cd * gamma_t * Bd^2  (4-6)

where Cd = a load coefficient, gamma_t = the total unit weight of the soil, and Bd = the width of the trench.

The value of Cd can be calculated as:

Cd = (1 - e^(-2*K*mu'*H/Bd)) / (2*K*mu')  (4-7)

where H = the depth of the trench above the top of the pipe, K = a lateral earth pressure coefficient, and mu' = the coefficient of friction for the trench fill.

Recommended values of gamma_t, K, and mu' for use with this equation are provided in Table 4-3 as summarized by Moser (1990).
key_points: Marston-Spangler method is used to estimate dead load on rigid pipe in a trench
Load per length of pipe depends on load coefficient Cd, total unit weight, and trench width squared
Cd depends on trench depth, lateral earth pressure coefficient, and coefficient of friction
Recommended values for soil parameters are provided in Table 4-3

equations.description: Calculates the dead load per unit length of rigid pipe in a trench using the Marston load theory
Calculates the load coefficient Cd for rigid pipe loading based on trench depth, lateral earth pressure coefficient, and friction

tables: Table 4-3: Recommended Values for Trench Load Coefficient (after Moser 1990)
sections.applicability: Applies to the calculation of dead loads on rigid pipes (concrete, cast iron) buried in trenches.

sections.title: Live Load
sections.body:
The primary live loads considered in the design of buried pipes are those from vehicles, including trucks, railroad, and airplanes. The stress at the top of the pipe is typically calculated using Boussinesq theory multiplied by an impact factors that account for dynamic effects. The equations presented in Table 4-2 can be used to estimate the vertical stress transferred to the top of the pipe from surface loading. Appropriate live load impact factors are summarized in Table 4-4.

Live load pressures (including an impact factor of 1.5) are summarized in Table 4-5. The values in this table indicate that the changes in stress become negligible below depths of 8 feet, 30 feet, and 24 feet for standard truck, railroad, and airport loads, respectively.
key_points: Live loads from trucks, railroad, and airplanes are primary considerations for buried pipe design
Boussinesq theory with impact factors is used to calculate live load stress at the pipe
Impact factors are provided in Table 4-4 for highway, railway, runway, and taxiway/apron conditions
Live load pressures become negligible below 8 ft (truck), 30 ft (railroad), and 24 ft (airport)
tables: Table 4-4: Impact Factors for Live Loading of Buried Pipe (from American Lifelines Alliance 2001)
Table 4-5: Live Load Pressures from Various Vehicle Loading (after American Lifelines Alliance 2001)
sections.applicability: Applies to the calculation of live loads from vehicles on buried rigid pipes, using Boussinesq theory with impact factors.

sections.title: Vertical Loads on Flexible Pipe
sections.body: Flexible pipes include corrugated metal, plastic, and thin-wall smooth steel pipes. These pipes deform when loaded and develop horizontal restraining pressures on the sides that may be approximately equal to the vertical pressure if the backfill is well-compacted. The vertical pressure on the top of the pipe depends on the surrounding soil. In highly compressible soil, the vertical pressure may exceed the overburden pressure. In contrast, arching in coarse-grained soils may significantly reduce the overburden pressure.
key_points: Flexible pipes include corrugated metal, plastic, and thin-wall smooth steel
Flexible pipes deform and develop horizontal restraining pressures
In compressible soil, vertical pressure may exceed overburden pressure
Arching in coarse-grained soils may significantly reduce overburden pressure on flexible pipe
sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of vertical loads on flexible pipes (corrugated metal, plastic, thin-wall steel) buried in soil.

sections.title: Dead Load
sections.body:
For very flexible pipe with outside diameter (Bc) the Marston load theory predicts a load (Wc) of:

Wc = Cd * gamma_t * Bc * D  (4-8)

where Cd = the load coefficient for rigid pipe (see Equation 4-7), gamma_t = the total unit weight of the trench backfill, and D = the outer diameter of the pipe (Moser 1990).

This method assumes that the pipe stiffness and soil stiffness are equal, which may lead to unconservative values of Wc.

The prism load is a more conservative approach for determining the dead load on a buried flexible pipe. The prism load (Wp) is simply the total weight of the soil above the pipe and is equal to:

Wp = gamma_t * H * D  (4-9)

where gamma_t = the backfill total unit weight, H = the depth of soil cover, and D = the outer diameter of the pipe.
key_points: Marston load theory for flexible pipe assumes pipe and soil stiffness are equal, which may be unconservative
Wc depends on the load coefficient Cd, total unit weight, pipe diameter, and outer diameter
The prism load is a more conservative approach: total weight of soil above the pipe
Prism load equals total unit weight times depth of cover times outer pipe diameter

equations.description: Calculates the Marston dead load on a flexible pipe based on load coefficient, unit weight, and pipe diameter
Calculates the prism load (conservative dead load) on a buried flexible pipe as the total weight of soil above the pipe

sections.applicability: Applies to dead load estimation on buried flexible pipes using Marston theory or the more conservative prism load method.

sections.title: Live Load
sections.body: The Boussinesq approach described in Section 4-4.2.2 should also be used to calculate live loads on flexible pipes.
key_points: Boussinesq approach with impact factors from Section 4-4.2.2 applies to live loads on flexible pipes
sections.applicability: Applies to the calculation of live loads on buried flexible pipes using Boussinesq theory with impact factors.

sections.title: Long Span Metal Culverts
sections.body:
The previously discussed methods do not apply to the calculation of stresses and design of long span metal culverts. The use of finite element analysis software specifically formulated for culverts, such as CANDE, is likely required. For additional guidance see Duncan (1979).

For the design of long span metal culverts, the engineer must distinguish between shallow and deep cover conditions (Duncan 1979). Shallow cover conditions apply to cases where the cover is less than one-fourth of the culvert span. Culverts with shallow cover must be designed for flexural stresses caused by live loads. The factor safety is calculated by comparing the predicted axial stresses and moment loading to the culvert capacity.

In contrast, deep cover conditions occur when the cover is greater than one-fourth of the span. Deep cover culverts only require design for ring compression, such that the seams don't collapse under the design loads. Design axial ring loads are higher than those calculated solely based on ring compression theory. This occurs because the culvert is much stiffer in ring compression than the surrounding soil and a negative arching condition occurs.
key_points: Standard pipe loading methods do not apply to long span metal culverts
Finite element software such as CANDE is likely required for long span culvert design
Shallow cover (less than one-fourth span) requires design for flexural stresses from live loads
Deep cover (greater than one-fourth span) requires design for ring compression only
Negative arching occurs because the culvert is stiffer in ring compression than surrounding soil
sections.applicability: Applies to the design and stress analysis of long span metal culverts with shallow or deep cover conditions.

sections.title: Deep Underground Openings
key_points: Parent section for the analysis of stresses on deep underground openings including tunnels and shafts
sections.applicability: General section heading for stress analysis of deep underground openings in rock and soil.

sections.title: General Factors
sections.body:
Prior to excavation of a tunnel, the rock or soil is typically at a state of equilibrium under the stresses imposed by overburden and external loads. Excavation disturbs that equilibrium condition and requires load to transfer to surrounding rock, soil, or tunnel support system. The soil and rock will always exhibit an immediate response to the changes in stress caused by the excavation. Often a time-dependent response also occurs, especially in saturated compressible soils. A good discussion of the development of equilibrium conditions during and after tunneling in soft ground, as well as tunneling and support methods, is provided in FHWA (2009).

Changes in stress are typically accompanied by displacement of the rock, soil, or support structure. Similar to retaining walls, some movement is desirable to create a suitable balance between the load carried by the structure and the load distributed to the soil. Due to the effects of this soil-structure interaction, the type of support system and tunneling method used will significantly affect the deformations experienced during and after tunneling, and therefore the loading imposed on tunnel support.

The stresses acting on an underground opening will also depend on the depth of the opening below the ground surface and the characteristics of the surrounding soil or rock. One common distinction between the terms deep and shallow compares the depth of cover to the diameter of the opening. Openings for which this ratio is less than 2 should be considered shallow and arching of the soil or rock should be ignored. Deep openings have a cover to diameter ratio greater than 3 and benefit from the effects of arching.

For deep underground openings, deformation toward the opening allows the release of stress and the development of arching in the surrounding soil or rock. For this reason, the stresses are heavily dependent on the amount of deformation allowed during construction and the degree of restraint provided by the lining.

Numerical methods, such as finite element analysis, can be used to calculate stresses and deformations of underground openings. These methods can be quite accurate and account for significant complexity provided the soil and rock are characterized properly and the construction sequence is adequately modeled. The methods presented in this section are useful for simple calculations and to check the results of more complex numerical models.
key_points: Excavation disturbs the equilibrium state and transfers load to surrounding ground or support system
Both immediate and time-dependent responses to stress changes occur
Some movement is desirable for soil-structure interaction balance
Cover to diameter ratio less than 2 is shallow (no arching); greater than 3 is deep (arching benefits)
Stresses depend on deformation allowed during construction and lining restraint
Numerical methods (FEA) can accurately calculate stresses if soil/rock and construction sequence are properly modeled
sections.applicability: Applies to the evaluation of stress conditions around deep underground openings during and after excavation in soil or rock.

sections.title: Openings in Rock
sections.body: Rock can be separated into two groups for the purposes of determining stresses: (1) sound, non-swelling rock that can sustain considerable tensile stress and (2) fractured, blocky, seamy, squeezing, or swelling rock. For more detailed explanations of rock properties, see Chapter 1. The behavior of these two groups is distinguished primarily by the ability of the rock to resist tensile stress and/or significant deformation.
key_points: Rock is grouped into sound non-swelling rock and fractured/blocky/seamy/squeezing/swelling rock
Distinction is based on the ability to resist tensile stress and significant deformation
Detailed rock properties are discussed in Chapter 1
sections.applicability: Applies to the classification of rock for determining stresses around underground openings.

sections.title: Sound Rock
sections.body:
Elastic analysis can be used to determine stresses surrounding tunnels or openings in intact, isotropic rock (e.g., crystalline igneous, homogeneous sandstone and limestone). Analytical methods are summarized in rock mechanics texts such as Goodman (1989).

For these materials, stresses in rock surrounding spheroidal cavities are lower than those for tunnels with the same cross-section. Elastic analysis can be used to determine the best arrangement of openings and pillars, such that supports are provided at locations of stress concentration.
key_points: Elastic analysis applies to stresses around openings in intact, isotropic rock
Applicable to crystalline igneous, homogeneous sandstone and limestone
Stresses around spheroidal cavities are lower than around tunnels of the same cross-section
Elastic analysis helps determine optimal arrangement of openings and pillars
sections.applicability: Applies to stress determination around underground openings in intact, isotropic, sound rock capable of sustaining tensile stress.

sections.title: Broken and Fractured Rock
sections.body: Pressure on tunnels in chemically or mechanically altered rock must be analyzed by approximate rules based on experience, such as those presented in Table 4-6. The rock conditions used in Table 4-6 are compared to other common rock quality indices in Table 4-7.
key_points: Broken and fractured rock requires empirical/experience-based approaches for tunnel pressure estimation
Table 4-6 provides approximate rock loads for various rock conditions
Table 4-7 compares rock conditions to RQD, Q index, and RMR
tables: Table 4-6: Approximate Overburden Rock Load Carried by Roof Support
Table 4-7: Approximate Relationship Between Rock Quality Indices (after Deere et al. 1970, Barton et al. 1974, Bieniawski 1990, Hemphill 2012)
sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of tunnel pressures in chemically or mechanically altered, broken, and fractured rock.

sections.title: Squeezing and Swelling Rock
sections.body:
Rocks in categories 7 to 9 of Table 4-6 and Table 4-7 are the result of clay deposits that have been heavily preloaded during their geologic history. The transition from very dense soil to soft rock is not well-defined. In some cases, very dense clays that have not fully lithified may be included in this category.

Rock properties are closely tied to the properties of the minerals from which it is comprised. The rocks in this category contain significant amounts of clay minerals with properties ranging from the non-swelling kaolinite group to the highly swelling montmorillonite group. Soil and rock that has a high fraction of clay minerals will tend to expand, absorb water, and lose shear strength while undergoing stress relief. Thus, rocks with significant amounts of clay minerals will tend to swell as a result of the stress relief around an underground opening. Swelling leads to a loss of shear strength and a tendency of the tunnel walls to squeeze into the opening.
key_points: Categories 7-9 of Table 4-6 involve heavily preloaded clay deposits that behave as squeezing/swelling rock
The transition from very dense soil to soft rock is not well-defined
Clay mineral content (kaolinite to montmorillonite) controls swelling behavior
Stress relief around openings causes swelling, loss of shear strength, and squeezing into the opening
sections.applicability: Applies to underground openings in squeezing and swelling rock containing significant clay minerals.

sections.title: Loads on Underground Openings in Rock
key_points: Parent section for methods to estimate vertical and horizontal loads on underground openings in rock
sections.applicability: General section heading for estimation of loads on underground openings in rock.

sections.title: Vertical Rock Load
sections.body: A common starting point for the estimation of vertical roof pressure is found in Table 4-6. It should be noted that the values presented in this table were largely based on observations by Terzaghi (1946) for tunnel widths in the range of 16 to 32 feet (5 to 10 meters) prior to the advent of "modern" tunneling methods. Table 4-6 provides an approximate means of calculating the vertical pressure or rock load that must be supported by roof lining. The height of rock (Hp) that must be supported is a function of the tunnel width (B) for high quality rock and also the tunnel height (Ht) for lower quality rock. The total vertical pressure can be found by multiplying Hp by the total unit weight of the rock.
key_points: Table 4-6 provides approximate vertical rock loads based on Terzaghi (1946) observations
Values were developed for tunnel widths of 16-32 feet prior to modern tunneling methods
Height of rock Hp to be supported depends on tunnel width B and height Ht depending on rock quality
Total vertical pressure is Hp multiplied by total unit weight of rock
sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of vertical roof pressure on tunnel supports in various rock conditions.

sections.title: Horizontal Pressures
sections.body: Horizontal pressures acting on a tunnel can be approximated using an active wedge type analysis, such as Coulomb, with the diagram shown at the bottom of Table 4-6. The vertical forces included in these calculations are the weight of the active wedge and the weight of the rock for a height (Hp) above the wedge. Shear strength parameters can be assumed or selected using guidance in Chapter 3. The critical inclination of the active wedge may be determined by either the shear strength of the rock or by the rock structure. The possibility of movement along a weak bedding plane or stratum should be considered.
key_points: Horizontal pressures on tunnels approximated using Coulomb active wedge analysis
Vertical forces include weight of active wedge and rock above for height Hp
Shear strength parameters from Chapter 3 or assumed values
Critical wedge inclination depends on rock shear strength or rock structure
Movement along weak bedding planes should be considered
sections.applicability: Applies to estimation of horizontal pressures on tunnel walls in rock using active wedge analysis.

sections.title: Other Methods for Tunnel Support Pressures
sections.body: Alternate empirical methods for estimating tunnel support pressures are available. The two most common are the rock tunneling quality index, Q, presented in Barton et al. (1974) and the rock mass rating system (e.g., Bieniawski 1976). These systems are described in more detail in Chapter 1. The roof pressure and support requirements for tunnels can be estimated from the value of Q and some of the joint properties. While not solely intended for tunneling applications, the RMR can be related to stand-up time, unsupported active span length, and roof pressure. See Bieniawski (1990) for additional comparison of methods for estimating tunnel support requirements.
key_points: Q system (Barton et al. 1974) and RMR system (Bieniawski 1976) are common empirical alternatives
Q index with joint properties can estimate roof pressure and support requirements
RMR relates to stand-up time, unsupported span length, and roof pressure
Bieniawski (1990) provides additional comparison of tunnel support estimation methods
sections.applicability: Applies to estimation of tunnel support pressures in rock using Q system or RMR system as alternatives to Terzaghi's method.

sections.title: Openings in Soft Ground (Soil)
key_points: Parent section for tunnel analysis in soft ground (soil) including ground behavior and support loads
sections.applicability: General section heading for underground openings in soft ground (soil).

sections.title: Ground Behavior
sections.body:
Selection of an appropriate method for tunnel construction in soft ground (i.e., soil tunneling) depends upon the response of the soil during and after excavation. This response is often referred to in terms of stand-up time, which is the amount of time the soil will support itself prior to the installation of tunnel supports. The stand-up time depends on the type of soil, the position of groundwater, and the size of the opening. Terzaghi's (1950) Tunnelman's Ground Classification provides a commonly used means of describing various types of ground response. The types of ground behavior for tunneling are summarized in Table 4-8.

In addition to the descriptions provided in Table 4-8, the behavior of fine-grained soils and silty sands above the water table can be evaluated using Table 4-9. The undrained stability factor (Ncrit) is used to assess the ground behavior as suggested by Peck (1969). This factor is defined as:

Ncrit = (sigma'_v - sigma_t) / su  (4-10)

where sigma'_v = effective overburden pressure at the tunnel centerline, sigma_t = interior applied pressure from compressed air or breasting, and su = undrained shear strength.

For coarse-grained soils, the ground behavior depends on the grain-size distribution, relative density, and the amount of clayey fines (binder) as indicated in Table 4-10. Uniform, loose materials (Cu < 3 and N < 10) with round grains run more freely than well-graded, dense materials (Cu > 6 and N > 30) with angular particles. Soils with properties between those listed in Table 4-10 will tend to exhibit intermediate ground behavior. Very high flowrates should be expected in tunnels below the water table through soils with relatively large particles, such as gravel and medium to coarse sand.
key_points: Stand-up time is the key parameter for soft ground tunnel construction method selection
Terzaghi's Tunnelman's Ground Classification (Table 4-8) describes ground response types: firm, raveling, running, flowing, squeezing, and swelling
Undrained stability factor Ncrit assesses fine-grained soil and silty sand behavior (Table 4-9)
Ncrit is defined as (effective overburden - interior pressure) / undrained shear strength
Coarse-grained soil behavior depends on grain-size distribution, relative density, and clayey fines (Table 4-10)
Loose, uniform materials run more freely than dense, well-graded materials

equations.description: Calculates the undrained stability factor for assessing ground behavior in fine-grained soils during tunneling

tables: Table 4-9: Ground Behavior for Clayey Fine-Grained Soils and Silty Sand (after FHWA 2009)
Table 4-10: Ground Behavior for Coarse-Grained Soils (after FHWA 2009)
sections.applicability: Applies to the assessment of ground behavior and stand-up time for tunnel construction in soft ground (soil).

sections.title: Soft Ground Support Loads
sections.body:
Support pressures on tunnels in soft ground are governed by many factors, including the unit weight of the overlying material, the groundwater level, soil properties, the amount deformation allowed during excavation, the interaction between soil and the supports, the opening shape, and the length of time between excavation and lining installation. Other factors should also be considered include the presence of other nearby openings, superimposed loads from neighboring structures, and the possibility of changes in groundwater conditions.

Figure 4-11 illustrates the loading mechanism surrounding soft ground tunnels. In coarse-grained soils, arching occurs above the tunnel. Arching transfers some of the overburden load to the surrounding ground so that only a portion of the total load above the tunnel is applied to the tunnel. In clay soils, undrained conditions tend to control. In this case, the undrained shear strength can be considered to provide support of a portion of the load above the tunnel.

A simplified approach to the selection of tunnel support loads is provided in Table 4-11 (FHWA 2009). More detailed guidance for the selection of tunnel support loads is summarized in Table 4-12. These tables are used by first determining the ground behavior type using Table 4-8 to Table 4-10.
key_points: Support pressures depend on unit weight, groundwater, soil properties, deformation allowed, soil-support interaction, opening shape, and timing
Nearby openings, neighboring structures, and groundwater changes must also be considered
Arching in coarse-grained soils reduces load on tunnel support
Undrained shear strength supports portion of load in clay soils
Table 4-11 provides simplified tunnel support loads; Table 4-12 provides detailed guidance
Ground behavior type from Tables 4-8 to 4-10 determines which support loads apply
figures: Figure 4-11: Loading Mechanisms for Soft Ground Tunneling
tables: Table 4-11: Simplified Tunnel Support Loads based on Ground Behavior (FHWA 2009)
Table 4-12: Soft Ground Tunnel Support Loads for H > 1.5*(B+Ht)
sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of support pressures for tunnels in soft ground (soil), considering arching, undrained strength, and ground behavior type.

sections.title: Loss of Ground
sections.body: As underground excavation is made, the surrounding ground starts to move toward the opening. These displacements occur as the soil around the opening expands due to stress release in addition to soil lost to the tunnel from raveling, runs, flows, etc. The resulting loss of ground causes settlement of the ground surface. The loss of ground associated with stress reduction can be predicted reasonably well, but the ground loss due to raveling, runs, flows, etc. requires a detailed knowledge of the subsurface conditions to avoid unacceptable amounts of settlement. A summary of methods to predict surface settlement resulting from lost ground can be found in FHWA (2009).
key_points: Ground moves toward the opening as excavation proceeds due to stress release and material loss
Loss of ground causes surface settlement
Stress-reduction-related ground loss can be predicted reasonably well
Ground loss from raveling, runs, and flows requires detailed subsurface knowledge
FHWA (2009) summarizes methods to predict surface settlement from ground loss
sections.applicability: Applies to the prediction of ground loss and surface settlement caused by underground excavation in soft ground.

sections.title: Pressure on Vertical Shafts
sections.body: In contrast to the methods presented in Section 4-3, the stress calculations for vertical shafts represent either active or passive earth pressure. These limiting earth pressure conditions correspond to a plastic rather than elastic state of stress within the soil.
key_points: Vertical shaft stress calculations use active or passive earth pressure (plastic conditions)
This contrasts with the elastic methods in Section 4-3
sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of earth pressures on vertical shafts using limiting (plastic) earth pressure conditions.

sections.title: Shafts in Coarse-Grained Soil
sections.body:
During excavation of a vertical cylindrical shaft in coarse-grained soil, the horizontal pressures around the shaft approach active earth pressure values. If outward-directed forces from a structure (e.g., buried silo) move the structure walls into the soil, the earth pressures will approach passive conditions. Earth pressures are discussed in more detail in DM 7.2.

Active earth pressures for cylindrical shafts have been determined using analytical, limit equilibrium, slip line, numerical, and experimental methods. The active earth pressure coefficient depends on the shaft dimensions and the soil strength. For shallow shafts (i.e., depth <= two diameters), theoretical solutions tend to be applicable while the effects of horizontal arching become significant at greater depths (Tobar and Meguid 2010). Horizontal arching is taken into account in some solutions by the coefficient lambda, which is the ratio of the circumferential stress to the vertical stress. The value of lambda is equal to 1 in analytical solutions, such as Terzaghi (1943) but may be as low as K0. Cheng et al.'s (2007) solution is plotted in Figure 4-12 for lambda = 1 and lambda = K0.

Active pressures must be modified if rigid bracing at the top of the shaft prevents development of an active state. For restrained vertical shafts, horizontal pressures may be as large as the at-rest pressure on a long wall with plane strain conditions.
key_points: Horizontal pressures on excavated shafts in coarse-grained soil approach active earth pressure
Outward-directed forces cause passive earth pressure conditions
Active earth pressure coefficient depends on shaft dimensions and soil strength
Shallow shafts (depth <= 2 diameters) follow theoretical solutions; deeper shafts are affected by horizontal arching
Lambda coefficient accounts for horizontal arching (ranges from K0 to 1)
Restrained shafts may experience at-rest pressures on plane strain conditions
figures: Figure 4-12: Radial Stress at the Sides of a Vertical Shaft in Sand (based on Cheng et al. 2007)
sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of earth pressures on vertical cylindrical shafts excavated in coarse-grained soils.

sections.title: Shafts in Clay
sections.body:
No support is needed from the ground surface to a depth of zcrit for shafts in clay. The critical depth (zcrit) is:

zcrit = 2*su / gamma_t  (4-11)

where su = the undrained shear strength of the soil and gamma_t = the total unit weight of the soil.

At greater depths, the ultimate horizontal pressure (sigma_h) on a shaft lining in soft clay can be estimated as:

sigma_h = gamma' * z - su  (4-12)

where gamma' = effective unit weight of the soil, z = depth below the ground surface, and su = undrained shear strength of the soil.

This pressure will likely occur after several months of unsupported excavation. The stability factors for fine-grained soils in Table 4-9 can be used as guidelines for the behavior of vertical shafts in clay.

In stiff, intact or fissured clays, the initial horizontal stress on vertical shaft walls will be small. Over time the pressure may increase to a value several times larger than the effective vertical stress (and ultimately to the swelling pressure if the shaft lining is sufficiently rigid). Local experience is important to provide useful information for soil pressures on vertical shafts in stiff clays.
key_points: No support needed above critical depth zcrit = 2*su / gamma_t for shafts in clay
Below critical depth, ultimate horizontal pressure equals effective unit weight times depth minus undrained shear strength
Ultimate pressure develops after several months of unsupported excavation
Table 4-9 stability factors apply as guidelines for vertical shaft behavior in clay
In stiff/fissured clays, pressure may increase over time to several times effective vertical stress
Local experience is important for stiff clay shaft design

equations.description: Calculates the critical depth above which no support is needed for a shaft in clay
Estimates the ultimate horizontal pressure on a shaft lining in soft clay at depths below the critical depth

sections.applicability: Applies to the estimation of earth pressures on vertical shafts in clay soils, including determination of unsupported critical depth.

sections.title: Numerical Solutions for Stresses in Soil
sections.body:
The analytical and chart-based solutions presented in this chapter are an excellent starting point for evaluation of stresses within a soil mass. However, their applicability is limited by the constraints and assumptions of each. These methods also struggle to effectively model complex subsurface profiles and loading conditions.

Computer programs and numerical solutions are an important part of geotechnical engineering practice. This section provides a brief overview of the application of numerical methods to the evaluation of stresses.
key_points: Analytical and chart solutions are limited by their assumptions and constraints
Numerical methods are important for complex subsurface profiles and loading conditions
This section provides an overview of numerical methods for stress evaluation
sections.applicability: Applies when analytical and chart-based stress solutions are insufficient due to complex subsurface or loading conditions.

sections.title: Numerical Analysis Types
sections.body:
Some computer programs (e.g., Settle3D, CONSOL, SETOFF) are available that directly rely upon elastic solutions, such as those presented in this chapter, to calculate changes in stress. These programs are specifically formulated for the solution of consolidation settlement problems discussed in the next chapter. The benefit provided by these programs is the automated calculation of changes in stress and the ability to consider time-dependent changes. However, the solutions depend on the same assumptions as the elastic solutions on which they are based.

Many continuum-based numerical analysis techniques are available. The most common of these in geotechnical engineering are the finite element and finite difference methods, with the former being somewhat more popular for stress analysis problems. These approaches divide the soil or rock into elements or grid points. The relationships between the external and gravitational forces acting on the elements (or grid) and the corresponding displacements are defined using constitutive (stress-strain) laws and failure criteria.

The following sections provide a condensed overview focused on the calculation of stresses using the finite element method. The use of finite element analysis (FEA) to determine stresses is relatively straight-forward. Calculation of accurate deformations requires significantly more expertise and experience. For a practical introduction to the use of FEA in geotechnical engineering see Bradley and VandenBerge (2015). A more in-depth perspective can be found in the books by Potts and Zdravkovic (1999, 2001).
key_points: Programs like Settle3D, CONSOL, SETOFF use elastic solutions for automated stress and consolidation calculations
These programs share the same assumptions as the underlying elastic solutions
Finite element and finite difference methods are the most common continuum-based approaches
FEA is relatively straightforward for stress calculation but requires more expertise for deformations
Bradley and VandenBerge (2015) provides a practical FEA introduction; Potts and Zdravkovic (1999, 2001) provides in-depth coverage
sections.applicability: Applies to the selection of numerical analysis methods for stress evaluation, including elastic solution-based programs and finite element/finite difference methods.

sections.title: Linear Elastic Stress Analysis
sections.body: The simplest FE analyses use linear elastic constitutive theory, which relates changes in stress linearly to strains (or displacements). For a linear elastic analysis, the only required material parameters are the elastic modulus, E, and Poisson's ratio, nu (or any other two elastic constants such as shear modulus or bulk modulus). For problems with only one material type (and one value of E), the calculated stresses will be independent of the value of E selected. However, when more than one material type is present, the relative values of E assigned to each material in the analysis can impact the calculated stresses because of arching and similar phenomena.
key_points: Linear elastic FEA relates stress changes linearly to strains
Only required parameters are elastic modulus E and Poisson's ratio nu
For single material problems, calculated stresses are independent of E value
For multiple materials, relative E values affect calculated stresses due to arching
sections.applicability: Applies to finite element stress analysis using linear elastic constitutive theory for simple to moderately complex problems.

sections.title: Nonlinear Elastic Stress Analysis
sections.body:
The stress-strain behavior of geological materials is truly linear over only a small range of strains. A properly selected nonlinear constitutive model will provide a more accurate prediction of behavior but will require additional input parameters and expertise. VandenBerge et al. (2014) found that major principal effective stresses calculated for embankments with linear elastic analysis were typically within 10% of the values calculated using more rigorous and time-consuming nonlinear procedures.

One of the earliest and most common nonlinear constitutive theories for soil is the hyperbolic model proposed by Duncan and Chang (1970) and described in more detail in Duncan et al. (1980). This model can also consider stress dependent variations in Poisson's ratio (or bulk modulus). It can be used with either effective stress (drained) or total stress (undrained) problems, provided the model parameters are determined using the appropriate type of test.

The Duncan-Chang model is based on the following observations:
- The principal stress difference (sigma_1 - sigma_3) tends to vary in a hyperbolic manner with strain,
- The initial modulus (Ei) increases with increased confining stress in a manner that can be described by a power function,
- The ultimate value of (sigma_1 - sigma_3) predicted by the hyperbola tends to be greater than the value measured by the test,
- The bulk modulus (Bt) of soil increases with increased confining stress in a manner that can be described by a power function.

Soil tends to respond in a stiffer, approximately linear manner with modulus (Eur) when unloaded and reloaded after some amount of shearing. The required parameters are summarized and illustrated in Table 4-13 and Figure 4-13.
key_points: Geological materials are truly linear over only a small strain range
Nonlinear models provide more accuracy but require more parameters and expertise
Linear elastic stresses for embankments are typically within 10% of nonlinear results
Duncan-Chang hyperbolic model is one of the earliest and most common nonlinear soil models
Model parameters include K, n, Rf, Kb, m, and Kur for initial modulus, bulk modulus, and unload-reload behavior
Model can be used for both drained and undrained conditions with appropriate test parameters
figures: Figure 4-13: Parameters Used in Duncan-Chang Model
tables: Table 4-13: Summary of Model Parameters for Duncan-Chang Model
sections.applicability: Applies to nonlinear elastic finite element stress analysis using the Duncan-Chang hyperbolic constitutive model for soil.

sections.title: Numerical Modeling Best Practice
sections.body:
Both linear and nonlinear finite element analysis can be used to make accurate predictions of stresses. The following guidelines have been found to yield the most consistent and uniform stress predictions (VandenBerge et al. 2014).

- Use isoparametric elements (i.e., 8-noded rectangles or 6-node triangles).
- Use a uniform mesh with elements of approximately the same shape, especially within any zones of interest.
- Use elements with an appropriate aspect ratio, preferably longest to shortest dimension, less than or equal to five.
- Keep the element size as small as practical with respect to the overall dimensions. A maximum element height of approximately 1 to 2% of the height of the problem domain is preferred.
- Remember to include the boundary water pressures from any impounded water present in the model.
key_points: Use isoparametric elements (8-noded rectangles or 6-node triangles)
Use uniform mesh with elements of similar shape in zones of interest
Element aspect ratio should be 5 or less (longest to shortest dimension)
Element height should be approximately 1-2% of the problem domain height
Include boundary water pressures from impounded water in the model
sections.applicability: Applies to best practices for finite element mesh design and modeling to achieve consistent stress predictions.

sections.title: Initial or Geostatic Stresses
sections.body:
The initial stress state in a FE model is dependent on the process used to "turn on" gravity and stress within the model. Vertical stresses are governed mostly by gravity loading. As the mesh deforms in response to gravity, horizontal stresses will develop and tend toward at rest (K0) conditions for a level, laterally-constrained mesh. For a linear elastic model, the value of K0 will be equal to nu / (1-nu). Calculation of initial horizontal stresses in this manner will yield correct results, and K0 will be less than 1.0, which is always the case for primary loading. The calculation of initial horizontal stresses in this way will lead to initial deformation of the model and the layer thicknesses may no longer match the in situ conditions. These displacements are a numerical artifact and should be zeroed or removed prior to examining the effects of new loading conditions. Overconsolidated conditions with K0 greater than 1.0 can be modelled by loading and then unloading the model, following the process by which K0 > 1.0 conditions occur in nature.

In many cases, the details of the initial stress process are program specific. The engineer using FEA should become familiar with the various options available so that appropriate methods are applied.
key_points: Initial FE stress state depends on how gravity is applied in the model
For linear elastic models, K0 = nu / (1-nu) for laterally-constrained level mesh
K0 less than 1.0 applies for primary loading conditions
Initial gravity-induced displacements are numerical artifacts and should be zeroed before applying new loads
Overconsolidated K0 > 1.0 can be modeled by loading and unloading the model
Details of initial stress procedures are program-specific
sections.applicability: Applies to the establishment of initial (geostatic) stress conditions in finite element models of soil.

sections.title: Staged Construction or Stress History
sections.body:
Finite element analysis allows the sequence of loading and construction staging to be modeled numerically. To a lesser extent, geologic stress history can also be modeled. Within the model, this occurs by adding and subtracting elements (or their weight) in steps. Staged models are especially important for nonlinear analysis because the properties of the material change with stress level.

For example, a staged approach is required to predict stresses and displacements around open excavations and tunnels. The initial ground conditions should be modeled after which the effects of removing soil or rock can be considered.

For cases where only stress distributions are required, such staging is unnecessary in linear elastic analysis. The use of a staged model is required, even for linear elasticity, to predict correct patterns displacement.
key_points: FEA allows numerical modeling of construction staging and loading sequence
Elements are added/subtracted in steps to simulate construction
Staged models are essential for nonlinear analysis due to stress-dependent properties
Staged approach is required for excavation and tunnel modeling
Staging is unnecessary for stress-only linear elastic analysis but required for correct displacement patterns
sections.applicability: Applies to finite element modeling of construction sequences, excavations, and stress history effects on soil behavior.

sections.title: Evaluation of Stress Due to Applied Loads
sections.body:
Changes in stress due to applied loads can be evaluated using a staged FE model. The first stage(s) of the model are used to create the desired initial state of stress that best represents the in situ conditions. At this point, the new loading can be added to the model in various forms, including distributed loads, point loads, and new soil layers. The predicted changes in stress can then be evaluated by comparing the predicted stress at convenient points within the model between subsequent stages. Where possible, the changes in stress predicted by FE models should be checked with analytical solutions such as those presented earlier in this chapter.

Engineers should be aware of the limitations of their numerical analyses. For example, two-dimensional FEA are useful for predicting changes in stress below long foundations, embankments, and large area fills because such problems can be analyzed in a plane strain manner. However, a three-dimensional program would be required to predict changes in stress below more complex conditions, such as a rectangular foundation.
key_points: Staged FE models establish initial stress conditions then add new loads
Changes in stress are evaluated by comparing stresses between subsequent stages
FE results should be checked against analytical solutions where possible
2D FEA is suitable for plane strain conditions (long foundations, embankments, large fills)
3D FEA is required for complex conditions such as rectangular foundations
sections.applicability: Applies to the use of staged finite element models to evaluate changes in stress from applied loads, with appropriate dimensionality (2D or 3D).

sections.title: Evaluation of Stress within Embankments and Slopes
sections.body:
The calculation of stresses is more complex for slopes and embankments compared with relatively level ground. First, no closed-form analytical solution is available for comparison because the soil in a slope is not laterally restrained. The lack of lateral restraint also means that K0 conditions will not be present, especially close to the face of a slope.

Stresses near natural slopes are best evaluated by starting with level ground in the FE model and progressively removing (excavating) elements to form the slope. Multiple stages of analysis may be required to establish the initial conditions. The removal of elements mimics the process by which the slope was formed in nature.

Likewise, stresses in an embankment can be modeled by adding layers of elements in stages. The fill zone can be "built" within the FE model in thin layers, mimicking the actual construction process. Deformations caused by the initial application of gravity loading should preferably be removed. However subsequent deformations of each layer of fill under the weight of the overlying material are realistic. This approach allows the true pattern of displacements within the embankment to be examined.
key_points: Stress calculation is more complex for slopes and embankments than level ground
No closed-form solution exists for slopes because soil is not laterally restrained
K0 conditions do not apply near slope faces
Natural slopes are modeled by progressively removing elements from level ground
Embankments are modeled by adding fill layers in stages mimicking construction
Initial gravity deformations should be removed; subsequent fill deformations are realistic
sections.applicability: Applies to finite element evaluation of stresses within embankments and slopes where K0 conditions and closed-form solutions are not available.

sections.title: Notation
sections.body: B = Width of a foundation, loaded area, or tunnel. Bc = Diameter of a flexible pipe. Bd = Width of trench in pipe loading calculations. Bt = Bulk modulus of soil. Cd = Load coefficient in pipe loading calculations. Cu = Coefficient of uniformity (from grain-size distribution). D = Outer diameter of pipe. E = Elastic modulus. EA = Active earth pressure force. Ei = Initial tangent modulus. Eur = Unload-reload modulus for Duncan-Chang model. hp = Pressure head. H = Depth of soil cover or vertical distance between ground surface and tunnel roof. Hp = Design load thickness in terms of depth. Ht = Tunnel height. I = Influence factor for change in stress calculations. Ka = Active earth pressure coefficient. Kb = Bulk modulus parameter for Duncan-Chang model. K0 = At-rest earth pressure coefficient. Kp = Passive earth pressure coefficient. Kur = Unload-reload modulus parameter Duncan-Chang model. N = Standard Penetration Test blow count. Ncrit = Undrained stability factor. pc = Tunnel air pressure. p'f = Center of Mohr circle at failure (MIT stress path space). Pa = Atmospheric pressure. u = Pore water pressure. qf = Radius of Mohr circle at failure. q0 = Applied pressure or load. Q = Rock tunneling quality index. r = Horizontal distance from centerline of a foundation. Rf = Reduction factor for Duncan-Chang model. RMR = Rock mass rating. RQD = Rock quality designation. su = Undrained shear strength. t = Stand up time for tunneling in raveling soils. T = Elapsed time between excavation and completion of permanent structure. Wc = Flexible pipe load. Wd = Rigid pipe load. Wp = Prism load on pipe. z = Depth below an applied load. zcrit = Critical depth for unsupported shafts in clay soils. Zi = Soil layer thickness. alpha = Angle between the major principal plane and the plane of interest. delta_sigma_z = Change in vertical stress. phi' = Effective stress friction angle. gamma' = Effective unit weight. gamma_t = Total unit weight. gamma_w = Unit weight of water. lambda = Ratio of the circumferential stress to the vertical stress. mu' = Coefficient of friction for trench backfill. nu = Poisson's ratio. sigma_1 = Major principal stress. sigma_2 = Intermediate principal stress. sigma_3 = Minor principal stress. sigma_h = Total horizontal stress. sigma'_h = Effective horizontal stress. sigma_t = Interior tunnel pressure from compressed air or breasting. sigma_v = Total vertical stress. sigma'_v = Effective vertical stress.
